summary: Iceland applies Schengen rules through its EEA/EFTA membership: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities get 90 days in any 180-day period (with ETIAS being phased in), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa — often applied for via another Schengen state representing Iceland.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

fee.notes: €90 (children 6–11: €45; under 6: free), paid in local currency where you apply. Iceland has few missions abroad — in many countries applications are handled by another Schengen state representing Iceland.

fee.notes: Approximate — Iceland handles stays over 90 days (work, study, family) through residence permits issued by the Directorate of Immigration rather than long-stay visas. Confirm the current fee and process before applying.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU/EEA visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

proofOfFunds.text: The Directorate of Immigration expects visitors to show sufficient funds for their stay. The reference amount is set in ISK per day plus a base amount per trip and is revised periodically; confirm the current figures with the Directorate of Immigration or an Icelandic mission.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash worth €10,000 or more (or the equivalent in other currencies) must be declared to customs when entering or leaving Iceland.

notes: Strict biosecurity rules: raw meat and unpasteurised dairy from outside the EEA may not be brought in, and used riding, angling and hunting gear must be disinfected and certified before arrival.
Alcohol allowances are limited and strictly enforced. Many arrivals use the duty-free store in Keflavík airport, where prices are far below city retail.

payments.text: Iceland is effectively cashless. Cards and contactless payments are accepted everywhere, from fuel pumps and buses to remote guesthouses. There is no need to withdraw krónur for a normal visit.

safety.text: Iceland has one of the lowest crime rates in the world. The real risks are natural: rapidly changing weather, wind-blown car doors, unstable volcanic areas and dangerous surf at beaches like Reynisfjara — follow safetravel.is guidance.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Iceland travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: June–August brings the midnight sun, open highland roads and the best hiking; September and February–March offer good northern-lights odds with milder crowds — winter travel needs flexible plans around storms.

idp.text: Iceland is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Iceland yet.

tips.text: Weather can turn dangerous within hours in any season. Check road.is and safetravel.is daily, never drive marked F-roads without a suitable 4x4, and be ready to change plans around storms.
Gravel chips, sandstorms and wind-torn car doors are the classic rental-car claims in Iceland — hold doors firmly in wind and consider gravel and sand/ash protection when hiring a car.
Iceland applies EU border systems: non-EU visitors are registered in the Entry/Exit System at the border, and the ETIAS travel authorization is being phased in for visa-exempt travelers.
Iceland is expensive — self-catering from Bónus or Krónan supermarkets, filling water bottles from the tap (it is excellent) and buying any alcohol at the airport duty-free store keep costs down.
Do not exchange money before arrival — every payment, down to public toilets and parking, is card or app based, and foreign cash is hard to spend.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Iceland?
faq.answer: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of around 60 countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa (€90); in many countries another Schengen state handles applications on Iceland’s behalf.

faq.question: Is Iceland in the Schengen Area even though it is not in the EU?
faq.answer: Yes. Iceland is not an EU member but participates fully in Schengen through its EEA/EFTA membership — the same visa rules, the shared 90-days-in-180 allowance and the EU border systems (EES, ETIAS) all apply.

faq.question: Do I need ETIAS to visit Iceland?
faq.answer: Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, visa-exempt non-EU travelers will need the €20 online authorization before traveling to Iceland and the rest of the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU ETIAS site for the current status.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for an Icelandair or PLAY stopover in Iceland?
faq.answer: If you leave the airport, normal Schengen entry rules apply — visa-exempt nationals can stop over freely within their 90/180-day allowance, while visa-required nationals need a Schengen visa even for a one-day stopover. Transit without leaving the international zone generally needs nothing extra for most nationalities.

faq.question: Is it safe to drive in Iceland in winter?
faq.answer: Main roads are kept open but storms close them at short notice, daylight is limited and ice is routine. Rent a 4x4, check road.is and safetravel.is every morning, and build slack days into any winter ring-road plan.
